segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics news digest for October 16th, 2026.
Catch up on Waymo's progress, Skild AI's developments in embodied intelligence, and the latest on humanoid robotics.
From Waymo Blog, "Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route"
details the launch of Waymo's autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, with a target for first riders in 2028.
The rollout is proceeding through a phased, safety-first approach, beginning with mapping and testing in collaboration with autonomous specialists.
This expansion is supported by a partnership with Element Fleet Management to establish job creation and fleet management solutions.
The autonomous driver technology has demonstrated significantly lower crash rates when operating within city environments compared to human drivers.
This progression aligns with Toronto's increasing mobility demands and Waymo's objective to provide a safer and more accessible transportation option.
The development signals continued progression in the application of autonomous technology within urban transportation systems.

From thesequence.substack.com, The Sequence Robotics - Issue number nine hundred fifty-two details Skild AI's research into transferring robotic intelligence across different hardware rather than rebuilding it for each machine.
The research focuses on motor adaptation, video-prompted task learning, and self-play to achieve this transferability.
The methodology involves attempting to separate intelligence from the physical body, positing that understanding a body should be learned by the model through experience.

The project investigates whether these capabilities can endure the practical constraints of speed, reliability, and safety during real-world deployment by having the intelligence inhabit unfamiliar machines.
This effort explores the potential for flexible intelligence across diverse physical systems.
The findings suggest a pathway toward more adaptable and broadly deployable artificial intelligence systems.
From Humanoid.guide, "PNDbotics Adam humanoid climbs 1 meter box, post claims".
This report details the successful climbing of a one-meter high box by the PNDbotics Adam humanoid.
The robot achieved this feat by analyzing the obstacle, planning movements, and executing a sequence of precise foot placements followed by a controlled weight transfer.
The maneuver required the robot to support and raise its body while maintaining equilibrium across the elevation change.

This capability was accomplished through coordinated movement across the entire body and a central weight transfer, following a detailed sequence of obstacle analysis, movement planning, foot placement, and weight shifting.
This demonstration indicates progress in developing complex locomotion and spatial reasoning for advanced humanoid robotics.
Further research into these multi-stage balance maneuvers is expected in the field of artificial intelligence and robotics development.
From Robohub, Robot Talk Episode 166 – Evolving robot bodies and brains, with Rika Antonova reports on the development of complementary robot hardware and algorithms using artificial intelligence.
Rika Antonova from the University of Cambridge contributed research focusing on co-design, automated algorithm discovery, and data-efficient reinforcement learning in robotics.
The work involved exploring methods for integrating artificial intelligence to create synergistic relationships between robot hardware and the software governing their operation.
Antonova's research methodology addresses the complex challenges of designing robotic systems where the physical embodiment and the computational intelligence are developed in tandem.
Findings from this research emphasize pathways for more efficient and intelligent robotic system creation.
This work signals a progression in creating more adaptive and capable autonomous machines.
From Planet ROS, "ROS Discourse General: Logging and Observability Guide Review Part 4 | Cloud Robotics WG Meeting 2026-10-19"
reports on the ongoing review of the Logging and Observability guide for the Cloud Robotics Working Group.
The session convened on Monday, October 19, 2026, at 4:00 PM UTC with the objective of finalizing the first draft of the guide.
The group proceeded with the editing process during this meeting, aiming to complete the guide's revisions and subsequently distribute it to guest speakers for review.
Information regarding meeting access and notifications is disseminated through established channels to encourage attendance for this collaborative effort.
This work advances the standardization of logging and observability practices within the cloud robotics domain.
And that's all the circuits for today!
Hope your algorithms are running smoothly.
Until tomorrow, keep building those brilliant ideas!
Peace out.
